title: When the Same Answer Costs Ten Times More
key_insight: Fast matrix work is like an efficient kitchen: group similar orders, keep ingredients nearby, and avoid moving the same supplies again and again.
body:
## The Same Recipe, Ten Times Faster

Two kitchens make the same meals, but one cooks plates singly while the other fills a whole oven tray. Batching works the same way: larger groups keep the computer busy with less repeated setup.

Engineers estimate the arithmetic with FLOPs, meaning individual number operations. But speed also depends on moving the numbers from memory, just as fetching ingredients can take longer than mixing them.

Memory layout means keeping numbers that are used together close together. Good batches and tidy layouts reduce fetching, while smaller number formats can save space if they keep enough detail for reliable results.
common_mistakes: Counting arithmetic alone — fetching numbers and starting many tiny jobs can take more time than the multiplication.
Assuming turning a grid sideways is always free — a later step may need to copy the numbers into a tidier order.
Making batches larger without checking waiting time and memory use.
Moving data between the main processor and graphics processor between nearby steps.
mini_exercise: Time 64 separate matrix jobs, then place the same 64 inputs in one batch and time one larger job. Check that both routes produce matching answers.
real_world_usage: Training and serving systems send matrix work to highly tuned processor libraries, then group compatible requests so the hardware spends more time calculating and less time setting up.
explain_back_prompt: Use the kitchen story to explain why batching and keeping nearby numbers together can make the same calculation finish sooner.
